name: Yauyos Quechua
confidence_why: 4 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 2 refine it); none contradicts.

new_statements.quote: As in the overwhelming majority of Quechuan languages, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a word (compare yanápa-n 'he helps' and yanapá-ya-n 'he is helping'; awá-rqa 'he wove' and awa-rqá-ni 'I wove'). The first syllable of a word with more than four syllables generally receives weak stress. There are two exceptions to this rule. First, in all dialects, exclamations often receive stress on the ultimate syllable (¡Achachák! 'What a fright!' ¡Achachalláw! 'How awful!'). Second, in those dialects where vowel length indicates the first person, stress falls on the ultimate syllable just in case person marking is not followed by any other suffix (uyari-yá-: 'I am listening', ri-rá-: 'I went'). (p. 23)
new_statements.citation: Shimelman, Aviva (2017). A grammar of Yauyos Quechua. Studies in Diversity Linguistics 9. Berlin: Language Science Press. 359 pp.
new_statements.locator: §2.2 'Syllable structure and stress pattern', p. 23 (p. 43); also §2.4.1 p. 27 (loan stress), p. 177 (-chuwan), §5 exclamations

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog penultimate stress (penultimate); adds initial weak/secondary stress in words of >4 syllables, final stress in exclamations and on word-final long 1st-person vowels, variable retention of Spanish stress in loans, and antepenultimate stress before final -chuwan. Describes the five southern dialects (amv, ach, ch, lt, sp) only.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the (suffixed) word, counted from the right edge; weak (secondary) stress on the initial syllable of words longer than four syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'The first syllable of a word with more than four syllables generally receives weak stress' (p. 23). On p. 27: words of five or more syllables may keep the original Spanish stress word-internally while the penult still carries Quechua stress (timblúr-wan-ráq-tri).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Exclamations often carry final stress in all dialects (¡Achachák!, ¡Achachalláw!; §5 adds that indigenous exclamations 'bear stress on the final syllable'). (2) In dialects marking 1st person by vowel length, stress is final when the long person-marking vowel is word-final (uyari-yá-:, ri-rá-:); fn. 4 notes this final-stress-on-length pattern holds for Huallaga but not Ancash or Huamalíes. (3) Spanish loans: speakers vary between keeping Spanish stress (kanásta-wan, fwíra-ta, mútu-qa) and restructuring to penult (tirruristá-wan, Kañití-ta, vaká-qa) (p. 27, Table 2.4). (4) 'If a word ends with -chuwan, stress is shifted to the antipenultimate syllable' (p. 177).
new_statements.identity_note: Shimelman 2017 covers only the five southern dialects of Yauyos Quechua (Apurí-Madeán-Viñac, Azángaro-Chocos-Huangáscar, Cacra-Hongos, Lincha-Tana, Liscay-San Pedro); the three northern dialects (Alis-Tomas, Huancaya-Vitis, Laraos) were extinct when she worked (p. 1). Taylor 1990 describes the northern Laraos dialect, which is exactly the variety Shimelman lacks; the final-stress-on-long-first-person-vowel exception is stated by Shimelman to hold only 'in those dialects where vowel length indicates the first person'.

audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant penult, not strict) rests on the 2017 LangSci reference grammar, the best and only full description of the language; the deciding sentence is verbatim at sec. 2.2 p. 23, and the stated exceptions (exclamations, dialectal 1sg-length ultima, -chuwan antepenult p. 178) are delimited classes consistent with dominant-not-strict penult. No instrumental or phonology-specific study exists to challenge it. Only housekeeping: the source PDF was not actually in custody (now saved under our files), the locator can be sharpened to 'sec. 2.2, p. 23', and the verify note's '-chuwan p. 177' should read p. 178.
